name: Dating-profile photo optimization

card.summary: Picking and ordering dating photos with data from strangers' votes; popular idea, little independent testing.
card.note: Forum reports of rated-best photos underperforming on apps are anecdotal.

quick.overview:
This is the practice of testing dating-app photos, usually with Photofeeler ratings, before choosing which to use. Supporters say it reveals how strangers see a photo.

Evidence is limited: the research comes from the company itself, and forum members report mixed real-world results.
quick.mechanism: People upload candidate photos to a rating site, compare scores on attractiveness, trustworthiness and smartness, and pick or order photos accordingly.[1]
quick.risks: Low physical risk. Reported drawbacks are bias toward certain expressions, discouraging scores, and sharing photos with strangers.[3]

lead: Dating-profile photo optimization is the practice of selecting, editing and ordering photographs for dating apps using feedback or data rather than personal preference alone. The aim is to present the best-looking, most appealing version of oneself in the pictures strangers see first, so that the face and physique people already have read at their strongest. In looksmaxxing communities it is most often associated with Photofeeler, a site where anonymous voters rate photos on attractiveness, trustworthiness and smartness [1][2].

Proponents say outside ratings reveal how strangers perceive a photo, since friends and family may give overly positive opinions [2]. The practice matters on swipe-based apps because photos carry more weight there than the written profile did on earlier dating services [7]. Forum members also report cases where their highest-rated photos did poorly on dating apps, and criticism that raters favour smiling expressions [3][4].

Photofeeler publishes its own analyses, including a 2014 study of business photos and a 2019 neural-network paper trained on 1.2 million dating photos [1]. No independent studies were found testing whether Photofeeler-optimised photos increase dating-app matches. Research on dating apps more broadly reports that photos and perceived attractiveness shape how many matches and messages a profile receives [5][7].

chain: Photos are tested with anonymous raters
Higher-scoring photos are chosen and ordered first
Profile presents the most favourable impression of looks
angle.text: People choose and order photos using stranger feedback so that their strongest, most flattering images lead a dating profile. The practice changes how looks are presented rather than the face or body itself.

infobox: Business (competent, likable, influential) and social (confident, authentic, fun) [1][2]
Percentile-style 1 to 10 scores within gender and age group, plus optional comments [2]
Earn karma by voting on others' photos, or buy credits [1][2]
Company-authored analyses; no independent trials found

paras: The practice involves choosing which photos to use on a dating profile, and in what order, by testing them with strangers. Photofeeler's dating test asks voters to rate a photo on smartness, trustworthiness and attractiveness [1]. The company's site describes the service as scoring photos on three dimensions, including an overall dateability measure, with voters leaving short notes through quick prompts, and a cycle of testing, applying suggestions and retesting to see how scores change [8].

Grokipedia says the site's founders wanted objective feedback because friends and family tend to be overly positive [2]. The company describes the audience as strangers, which is the point of the method: a dating-app viewer is also a stranger, and proponents say a stranger's first-glance impression is the relevant one [1][2].

sections.h: Photofeeler: history and how it works
paras: Photofeeler was founded in 2013 in Boulder, Colorado, by Ben Peterson and Ann Pierce, who was its first chief executive [1]. Grokipedia gives the founding month as May 2013, states that Peterson holds graduate degrees in algorithms from Carnegie Mellon University, and says the company joined the Boomtown accelerator in 2014 with small seed funding [2].

Users upload a photo, choose a category (dating, business or social) and receive numerical scores and anonymous comments from other users; each category scores three traits, and fraud filters and AI processing are used to protect the accuracy of the results [1]. Grokipedia states that scores run from 1 to 10 as percentiles within gender and age groups, so that 5 is average, are adjusted for how generously individual voters rate, and that free access is earned as karma by voting on others' photos while credits can be bought [2]. The company's homepage says photos are visible to voters only for the period the user chooses and lists Forbes, Today, Fast Company, Time and Business Insider among outlets that have featured the service [8].

The company also runs a blog called Profiled, which publishes photo tips and its own analyses [1]. Titles on the blog include posts on smiling and first impressions, a replication of an OkCupid study on men's photos, and a list of photo mistakes said to be backed by data; the blog index does not itself state their findings [9].

The company has published analyses of its own data. A 2014 study of more than 60,000 ratings of 800 business photos found that a smile showing teeth gave the largest boost to likability and that formal attire raised perceived competence and influence [1].

A 2019 paper by Agastya Kalra and Ben Peterson, presented at the International Conference on Image Analysis and Recognition, introduced Photofeeler-D3, a convolutional neural network trained on the company's dating dataset of 1.2 million photos and tens of millions of votes [1]. The authors reported that the model matched the accuracy of about ten human voters in predicting smartness, trustworthiness and attractiveness, and that its attractiveness output reached state-of-the-art results on standard facial-beauty benchmarks [1]. These results describe agreement between model and voters rather than success on dating apps.

Research on dating platforms offers background for why photo choice matters. A 2016 study by Gareth Tyson and colleagues at Queen Mary University of London that created Tinder profiles found that male profiles with three pictures received far more matches than those with none, and that men received a match on 0.6 percent of their likes against 10 percent for women [5][7]. OkCupid co-founder Christian Rudder reported in 2009 that the men rated most physically attractive by women received about 11 times as many messages as the least attractive [5]. A 2007 study cited on Wikipedia found that nine in ten participants had lied about at least one attribute in an online profile, weight being the most common [5].

Tinder was released in September 2012 and is credited with popularising swiping; Wikipedia notes it places more weight on photos than earlier services that relied on written profiles [7]. Wikipedia also notes that a 2012 review concluded matching algorithms of online dating services were only negligibly better than random pairing, and that attention is unevenly distributed, with a small share of users receiving most matches [5]. These findings concern profiles in general and do not test Photofeeler scores.

In general terms, people upload several candidate photos, compare scores and comments, and lead with the highest-scoring images, often repeating the process after changing lighting, expression, clothing or framing. Photofeeler's own materials describe separate tests for dating, business and social profiles because different traits matter in each [1][8].

Because scores are standardised against same-gender, same-age peers, Grokipedia says younger or older users are not marked down simply for their age group [2]. Members of looksmax.org discuss comparing results across voter settings and how the algorithm adjusts scores [4][6].

Grokipedia reports user criticisms that scores can run generous, that raters may vote quickly to earn credits, that conventional, approachable photos tend to score higher than edgier ones, and that some users see low-scoring photos receive more matches than high-scoring ones; the company has said its votes are real and AI-filtered and that the tool tests elements such as pose and angle rather than measuring personal appeal [2]. Grokipedia is AI-generated, and these points are reported as claims that circulate rather than measured findings.
The company's own research is self-published, and no independent study compares Photofeeler scores with dating-app outcomes [1][2].

Members of looksmax.org share Photofeeler scores and debate their usefulness. Reported complaints include a mismatch between rater scores and Tinder results and a perceived bias toward smiling photos [3]. Others compare results across voter-age and gender settings and discuss how the algorithm adjusts scores [4][6].

timeline.event: Tinder is released, popularising swipe-based dating built around photos [7].
Photofeeler is founded in Boulder, Colorado [1][2].
Photofeeler publishes an analysis of more than 60,000 ratings of 800 business photos [1].
A Queen Mary University of London study of Tinder profiles examines photos and matches [5][7].
Photofeeler-D3, a neural network trained on 1.2 million dating photos, is presented [1].

lore.intro: Photofeeler is the main reference point; forum members dispute how well its scores predict dating-app performance [3][6].

claims.claim: Rated-best photos do not necessarily perform best on dating apps
claims.believers: A poster said his highest-rated photo did poorly on Tinder while his lowest-rated did well [3].
claims.experts: No published study compares Photofeeler scores with dating-app outcomes; broader research shows photo count and attractiveness relate to matches [5].

claims.believers: Members say serious photos are marked down with requests to smile [3].
claims.experts: Photofeeler's own 2014 business-photo analysis found that a smile showing teeth gave the largest boost to likability [1].

claims.claim: Outside ratings are more honest than friends and family
claims.believers: Photofeeler's founders and users say friends and family tend to be overly positive, so anonymous voters give a truer read [2].
claims.experts: The 2019 Photofeeler paper reports the model matches averages of about ten human voters, which concerns agreement among raters rather than dating outcomes [1].

claims.claim: Scores are standardised, so they are comparable across age and gender
claims.believers: The company describes percentile scores relative to same-gender, same-age peers and adjusted for voter generosity [2].
claims.experts: The adjustment method is described by the company; independent validation has not been published [1][2].
